¶
'''theralite''' (ther′a-līt), ''n.'' See ''tephrite.''

'''therapeusis''' (ther-a-pū′sis), ''n.'' [NL., < Gr. θεραπεύειν, cure: see ''therapeutic.''] Therapeutics.

'''Therapeutæ''' (ther-a-pū′tē), ''n. pl.'' [NL., < Gr. θεραπευτής, an attendant, a servant: see ''therapeutic.''] According to ancient tradition, a mystic and ascetic Jewish sect in Egypt, of the first century.

'''therapeutic''' (ther-a-pū′tik), ''a.'' and ''n.'' [= F. ''thérapeutique'' = Sp. ''terapéutico'' = Pg. ''therapeutico'' = It. ''terapeutico,'' < NL. ''therapeuticus,'' curing, healing (fem. ''therapeutica,'' sc. ''ars''), < Gr. θεραπευτικός (fem. ἡ θεραπευτική, the art of medicine), < θεραπευτής, one who waits on another, an attendant, < θεραπεύειν, wait on, attend, serve, cure, < θεράπων, an attendant, servant.] '''I.''' ''a.'' Curative; pertaining to the healing art; concerned in discovering and applying remedies for diseases. Also ''therapeutical.''

{{smaller block|''Therapeutick'' or curative physick we term that which restoreth the patient unto sanity, and taketh away diseases actually affecting.{{right|''Sir T. Browne,'' Vulg. Err., iv. 13.}}}}

{{smaller block|All his profession would allowe him to be an excellent anatomist, but I never heard any that admired his ''therapeutique'' way.{{right|''Aubrey,'' Lives (William Harvey).}}}}

'''II.''' ''n.'' [''cap.''] One of the Therapeutæ. ''Prideaux.''

'''therapeutics''' (ther-a-pū′tiks), ''n.'' [Pl. of ''therapeutic'' (see ''-ics'').] That part of medicine which relates to the composition, the application, and the modes of operation of the remedies
readings.c1s2:
for diseases. {{smaller|It not only includes the administration of medicines properly so called, but also hygiene and dietetics, or the application of diet and atmospheric and other non-medicinal influences to the preservation or recovery of health.}}

'''therapeutically''' (ther-a̤-pū′ti-ka̤l-i), ''adv.'' In a therapeutic manner; in respect to curative qualities; from the point of view of therapeutics.

'''therapeutist''' (ther-a̤-pū′tist), ''n.'' [< ''therapeut(ics)'' + ''-ist.''] One who is versed in the theory or practice of therapeutics. Also ''therapist.''

'''theraphose''' (ther′a̤-fōs), ''n.'' and ''a.'' [< F. ''théraphose'' (NL. ''Theraphosa'', neut. pl.), appar. < Gr. θηράφιον, a dim. of θηρίον, a wild beast.] '''I.''' ''n.'' One of a division of spiders instituted by Walckenaer, containing large quadripulmonary spiders which lurk in holes, as the mygalids and the trap-door spiders; any latebricole spider (see ''Latebricolæ''). {{smaller|This division corresponds to the genus ''Mygale'' in a former broad sense, and to the modern ''Tetrapneumona'' (which see).}}

'''II.''' ''a.'' Noting a spider of the group above defined.

'''therapist''' (ther′a̤-pist), ''n.'' [< ''therap-y'' + ''-ist.''] Same as ''therapeutist.'' ''Medical News'', XLIX. 510.

'''therapod''' (ther′a̤-pod), ''a.'' and ''n.'' An erroneous form of ''theropod.''

'''Therapon''' (ther′a̤-pon), ''n.'' [NL. (Cuvier and Valenciennes, 1829), < Gr. θεράπων, an attendant, servant.] The typical genus of the fam-
readings.c1s3:
ily ''Theraponidæ'', containing such species as ''T. theraps''.

'''Theraponidæ''' (ther-a̤-pon′i-dē), ''n. pl.'' [NL. (Sir J. Richardson, 1848), < ''Therapon'' + ''-idæ''.] A family of percoideous acanthopterygian fishes, represented by the genus ''Therapon'' and related forms.

'''theraponoid''' (thẹ̄-rap′ọ̄-noid), ''a.'' and ''n.'' [< ''Therapon'' + ''-oid''.] '''I.''' ''a.'' Resembling a fish of the genus ''Therapon''; of or pertaining to the ''Theraponidæ''.

'''II.''' ''n.'' Any member of this family.

'''therapy''' (ther′a̤-pi), ''n.'' [= F. ''thérapie'', < Gr. θεραπεία, a waiting on, service, < θεραπεύειν, serve, attend: see ''therapeutic''.] The treatment of disease; therapeutics; therapeusis: now used chiefly in compounds: as, neuro''therapy''.

'''therbeforne†''', ''adv.'' A Middle English form of ''therebefore''.

'''there''' (ᴛ̵ʜãr), ''adv.'' and ''conj.'' [< ME. ''there. ther, thare, thar, thore'', < AS. ''thǣr, thēr'' = OS. ''thār'' = OFries. ''ther, der'' = MD. ''daer'', D. ''daar'' = MLG. ''dār'', LG. readings.c3s1:
¶
'''there''' (ᴛ̵ʜãr), ''interj.'' [By ellipsis from ''see there, look there, go there.''] Used to express: (''a'') Certainty, confirmation, triumph, dismay, etc.: as, ''there!'' what did I tell you?

{{smaller block|Let them not triumph over me. Let them not say in their hearts, ''There! there!'' so would we have it.
{{right|''Book of Common Prayer'', Psalter, Ps. xxxv. 25.}}}}

{{smaller block|Why, ''there, there, there, there!'' a diamond gone, cost me two thousand ducats! {{right|''Shak.'', M. of V., iii. 1. 87.}}}}

(''b'') Encouragement, direction, or setting on.

{{smaller block|Enter divers spirits, in shape of dogs and hounds, and hunt them about. . . .
''Pros.'' Fury, Fury! ''there'', Tyrant, ''there!'' hark!
{{right|''Shak.'', Tempest, iv. 1. 257.}}}}

(''c'') Consolation, coaxing, or quieting, as in hushing a child: as, ''there! there!'' go to sleep.

'''thereabout''' (ᴛ̵ʜãr′a-bout″), ''adv.'' [< ME. ''thereaboute, theraboute, tharaboute''; < ''there'' + ''about.''] 1†. About that; concerning that or it.

{{smaller block|Er that I go
What wol ye dine? I wol go ''thereaboute.''
{{right|''Chaucer'', Summoner's Tale, l. 129.}}}}

{{smaller block|And they entered in, and found not the body. . . . And it came to pass, as they were much perplexed ''thereabout'', behold, two men stood by them in shining garments.
{{right|Luke xxiv. 4.}}}}

2. Near that place; in that neighborhood.

{{smaller block|He frayned, as he ferde, at frekez that he met,
If thay hade herde any karp of a knyȝt grene,
In any grounde ''thar-aboute'', of the grene chapel.
{{right|''Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 703.}}}}

3. Near that number, quantity, degree, or time: as, a dozen or ''thereabout;'' two gallons or ''thereabout.'' In this and the last sense also ''thereabouts.''

''thar'' (for the expected *''thēr''), there, in that place; orig. a locative form (nearly like the dat. and instr. fem. sing. ''thǣre'') of the pronominal stem *''tha'', appearing in ''the'', ''that'', etc., also in ''then'', etc. Cf. ''here''1, ''where''; Skt. ''tarhi'', then, ''karhi'', when. In comp. ''there'' is the adverb in its literal use, or, in ''therein'', ''therefor'', etc., in a quasi-pronominal use, ''therein'' being 'in that (sc. place),' ''thereby'' being 'by that (sc. means),' etc. ''There'' is therefore explained by some as really the dat. fem. sing. of the AS. def. art., but such use of a fem. form (instead of the expected neuter), in such a way, is unexampled; and the explanation cannot apply to the similar elements ''here-'' and ''where-'' as used in composition.] '''I.''' ''adv.'' '''1.''' In or at a definite place other than that occupied by the speaker; in that place; at that point: used in reference to a place or point otherwise or already indicated or known: as, you will find him ''there'' (pointing to the particular place); if he is in Paris, I shall see him ''there''. {{smaller|It is often opposed to ''here'', ''there'' generally denoting the place more distant; but in some cases the words when used together are employed merely in contradistinction, without reference to nearness or distance.}} {{smaller block|Stand thou ''there'', or sit here under my footstool. {{right|Jas. ii. 3.}}}} {{smaller block|You have a house i' the country; keep you ''there'', sir. {{right|''Fletcher'', Loyal Subject, i. 3.}}}} {{smaller block|All life is but a wandering to find home; When we are gone, we're ''there''. {{right|''Ford and Dekker'', Witch of Edmonton, iv. 2.}}}} {{smaller block|Of this the ''there'' born Emperour Adrian received his name. {{right|''Sandys'', Travailes, p. 2.}} Darkness ''there'' might well
Seem twilight here. {{right|''Milton'', P. L., vi. 11.}}}} '''2.''' Into that place; to that place; thither: after verbs of motion or direction: as, how did that get ''there?'' I will go ''there'' to-morrow. {{smaller block|My heart stands armed in mine ear,
And will not let a false sound enter ''there.'' {{right|''Shak.'', Venus and Adonis, l. 780.}}}} {{smaller block|There was Lord Belfast, that by me past
And seemed to ask how should I go ''there?'' {{right|''Thackeray'', Mr. Molony's Account of the Ball.}}}} '''3.''' At that point of progress; after going so far or proceeding to such a point: as, you have said or done enough, you may stop ''there.''—'''4.''' In that state or condition of things; in that respect. {{smaller block|To die, to sleep;
To sleep: perchance to dream: ay, ''there'''s the rub. {{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, iii. 1. 65.}}}} {{smaller block|''Mary.'' Of a pure life?
''Renard.'' . . . Yea, by Heaven . . . You are happy in him ''there.'' {{right|''Tennyson'', Queen Mary, i. 5.}}}} '''5.''' Used by way of calling the attention to something, as to a person, object, or place: as, ''there'' is my hand. {{smaller block|Some wine, within ''there'', and our viands! {{right|''Shak.'', A. and C., iii. 11. 73.}}}} '''6.''' Used as an indefinite grammatical subject, in place of the real subject, which then follows the verb, increased force being thus secured: so used especially with the verb ''to be:'' as, ''there is'' no peace for the wicked. {{smaller block|A Knight ''ther was'', and that a worthy man. {{right|''Chaucer'', Gen. Prol. to C. T., l. 43.}}}} {{smaller block|And God said, Let ''there be'' light; and ''there was'' light. {{right|Gen. i. 3.}}}} {{smaller block|''There'' appears a new face of things every day. {{right|''Bacon'', Political Fables, ix., Expl.}}}} {{smaller block|''There'' seems no evading this conclusion. {{right|''H. Spencer'', Social Statics, p. 433.}}}} 7. Used like ''that'' in interjectional phrases: such as, ''there'''s a darling! ''there'''s a good boy! {{smaller block|Grandam will Give it a plum, a cherry, and a fig: ''There'''s a good grandam! {{right|''Shak.'', K. John, ii. 1. 163.}}}} {{smaller block|Do your duty, ''There'''s a beauty. {{right|''W. S. Gilbert'', Fairy Curate.}}}} 8†. Thence. {{smaller block|For in my paleys, paradys, in persone of an addre, Falseliche thow fettest ''there'' thynge that I loued. {{right|''Piers Plowman'' (B), xviii. 334.}}}} {{smaller|'''All there.''' See ''all.''—'''Here and there.''' See ''here''1.—'''Here by there†''', here and there. ''Spenser.''—'''Neither here nor there.''' See ''here''1.—'''That . . . there''', a colloquial pleonasm intended to emphasize the demonstrative use of ''that'' before its noun: as, ''that'' man ''there.'' In illiterate speech the noun is often transposed after ''there:'' as, ''that there'' boy.—'''To get there''', to succeed in doing something; be successful. [Slang.]}} '''II.'''† ''conj.'' (''rel. adv.'') Near that place; in that neighborhood. {{smaller block|He frayned, as he ferde, at frekez that he met, If thay hade herde any karp of a knyȝt grene, In any grounde ''thar-aboute'', of the grene chapel. {{right|''Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight'' (E. John Smith's'' Works, I. 106.}}}} '''thereabouts''' (ᴛ̵ʜãr′a-bouts″), ''adv.'' [< ''thereabout'' + adv. gen. ''-s.''] Same as ''thereabout'', 2 and 3. {{smaller block|Some weeke or ''thereabouts.'' {{right|''Heywood'', Fair Maid of the West (Works, ed. 1874, II. 275).}}}} {{smaller block|She could see the interior of the summer-house. . . . Clifford was not ''thereabouts.'' {{right|''Hawthorne'', Seven Gables, xvi.}}}} '''thereafter''' (ᴛ̵ʜãr-ȧf′tėr), ''adv.'' [< ME. ''therefter'', ''tharafter'' (= OS. ''tharafter'' = OFries. ''therefter'', ''derefter'' = D. ''daarachter'' = Sw. Dan. ''derefter''); < ''there'' + ''after''.] 1†. After that; after them. {{smaller block|Wol he have pleynte or teres or I wende? After that; afterward. {{smaller block|And whan thow hast thus don, departe for god, and for thy soule all thy tresour, for thow maiste not longe ''ther-after'' lyven. {{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. Three knights were ''thereamong''; and they too smiled.{{right|''Tennyson'', Pelleas and Ettarre.}}}} '''thereanent''' (ᴛ̵ʜãr′a̤-nent′), ''adv.'' [< ''there'' + ''anent''.] Concerning that; regarding or respecting that matter. [Scotch.] '''thereas†''' (ᴛ̵ʜãr-az′), ''conj.'' [< ME.
